FGs are two-dimensional models that represent the relationships between elements and their degree of membership using nodes and edges. Dealing with ambiguous data and discussing the nature of each edge in a FG can be complex when utilizing fuzzy theory. On the other hand, CFGs are an improved approach to FGs. The membership values of vertices and edges in a fuzzy graph are between 0 and 1, whereas CFGs are more significant because vertices and edges have both lower and upper IVF-membership values and F-membership values. These membership values can be any real number in the interval [0, 1]. CFGs are an effective approach to deal with inadequate information of relationships among areas and controlling information loss within a given system. An algorithm to identify the affecting areas due to tsunami threat is shown in Table 2. Consider the set X consisting of the areas a_(1), a_(2), a_(3), a_(4), a_(5) and a_(6), in the vicinity of an ocean where an earthquake takes place and these areas can be affected by tsunami. A tsunami threat model is developed with the help of CFG T = ( I , J ) shown in Fig 3. The IVF-memberships and F-memberships of the vertices of T = ( I , J ) and edges of T = ( I , J ) are given in Tables 3 and 4, respectively.

List of all possible paths including the strengths and the strengths of their connections between a_(1) and a_(2) in a CFG are given in Table 5. Here, the edge (a_(1), a_(2)) in CFG is cubic α−strong. Likewise, it would be worthwhile to investigate the nature of other edges between areas. Analyzing the characteristics of each edge in the CFG would further underscore the significance and efficacy of our research. Based on Fig 3 and conventional computations, the connectivity between vertices in T = ( I , J ) can be determined as follows: C O N N T - ( a 1 a 2 ) ∞ ( a 1 , a 2 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 2 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 1 a 3 ) ∞ ( a 1 , a 3 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 2 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 2 a 3 ) ∞ ( a 2 , a 3 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 3 ] , 0 . 3 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 2 a 4 ) ∞ ( a 2 , a 4 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 3 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 3 a 4 ) ∞ ( a 3 , a 4 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 3 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 3 a 5 ) ∞ ( a 3 , a 5 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 2 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 4 a 5 ) ∞ ( a 4 , a 5 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 2 , 0 . 3 ] , 0 . 3 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 4 a 6 ) ∞ ( a 4 , a 6 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 2 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 5 a 6 ) ∞ ( a 5 , a 6 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 2 , 0 . 3 ] , 0 . 3 ⟩ . (14)

The concept of partial cubic α-strong and δ−weak edges presents a fresh expansion of the current notion of cubic α-strong and cubic δ-weak edges within the framework of earthquake-induced tsunami threat modeling. Through this comparative examination, it can be suggested that partial cubic α-strong and δ−weak edges provide specific advantages in contrast to cubic α-strong and cubic δ-weak edges. C O N N T - ( a 1 a 2 ) ∞ ( a 1 , a 2 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 2 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 1 a 3 ) ∞ ( a 1 , a 3 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 2 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 2 a 3 ) ∞ ( a 2 , a 3 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 3 ] , 0 . 3 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 2 a 4 ) ∞ ( a 2 , a 4 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 3 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 3 a 4 ) ∞ ( a 3 , a 4 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 3 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 3 a 5 ) ∞ ( a 3 , a 5 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 2 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 4 a 5 ) ∞ ( a 4 , a 5 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 2 , 0 . 3 ] , 0 . 3 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 4 a 6 ) ∞ ( a 4 , a 6 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 1 , 0 . 2 ] , 0 . 2 ⟩ , C O N N T - ( a 5 a 6 ) ∞ ( a 5 , a 6 ) = ⟨ [ 0 . 2 , 0 . 3 ] , 0 . 3 ⟩ . (15) From Eq 15, when applying the concept of cubic α-strong, cubic β-strong, cubic δ-weak, partial cubic α-strong and partial cubic δ-weak edges to the tsunami threat model given in a Fig 3, specific edges can be identified with precision. These edges can be identified based on the satisfaction of the given edges conditions. Cubic α-strong edges are (a_(3), a_(5)), (a_(3), a_(4)), (a_(4), a_(6)), cubic β-strong edges are (a_(1), a_(2)), (a_(1), a_(3)), cubic δ-weak edges are (a_(4), a_(5)), (a_(5), a_(6)), partial cubic α-strong edge is (a_(2), a_(4)) and partial cubic δ− weak edge is (a_(2), a_(3)). In Cubic Fuzzy Graph, when we discuss only cubic strong and weak edges, we have the concept of cubic α-strong edge. This edge is such that if we remove it and then check the strength of connectivity, the IVF-connectivity is strictly less than the IVF-membership value of that edge. In terms of F-connectivity, it’s also strictly less than the F-membership value. However, in the condition of a cubic δ-weak edge, it’s strictly greater. But in the case of a cubic β-strong edge, the IVF-connectivity is equal to the IVF-membership value, and the F-connectivity is equal to the F-membership value. At times, we encounter cases where the IVF-connectivity is equal to the IVF-membership value, but the F-connectivity is strictly less or greater than the F-membership value, or the IVF-connectivity is strictly less or greater than the IVF-membership value while the F-connectivity is equal to the F-membership value. In such situations, the concept of cubic α-strong or cubic δ-weak edges cannot handle this. Therefore, in such conditions, the concept of partial cubic α-strong and partial cubic δ-weak edges plays an important role. It provides information not only about cubic α-strong, cubic β-strong and cubic δ-weak edges but also about the nature of the remaining edges. From Fig 3 and Eq 15, if we only consider the concepts of cubic α-strong, cubic β-strong and cubic δ-weak edges, we have cubic α-strong zones as (a_(3), a_(5)), (a_(3), a_(4)), (a_(4), a_(6)), cubic β-strong zones as (a_(1), a_(2)), (a_(1), a_(3)) and cubic δ-weak zones as (a_(4), a_(5)), (a_(5), a_(6)). However, the remaining edges that do not satisfy the conditions of these edges do not provide any information about their nature. Therefore, using the concepts of partial cubic α-strong and partial cubic δ-weak edges helps us understand the condition of the remaining edges. Hence, when viewed comparatively, the concept of partial cubic α-strong and δ-weak edges presents clear advantages over cubic α-strong and cubic δ-weak edges, particularly in terms of precise zone delineation and a thorough examination of tsunami conditions across past, present and future scenarios.

result.scope_note: Version 0.5.2 adds bounded model API response reads, strict semantic-review JSON parsing, typed reasoning-graph schema validation with versioned contract-aware fingerprints, source-reconstructed graph/node provenance, mandatory inference-to-claim links and empty-graph rejection, version-bound semantic-review 1.4 templates with legacy 1.0–1.3 fingerprint import support, separate raw-file and extracted-text SHA-256 provenance, exact source-hash file inventories with isolated pip-installed wheel and release-artifact verification, strict Content-Length grammar, and full-commit-SHA-pinned CI dependencies. Statistical output now states the common-variance assumptions and heteroskedasticity limitation of pooled-SD Cohen's d and classical Hedges' g. Version 0.5.1 hardened authenticated transport and strict model/statistics JSON, improved Welch numerical stability, and stabilized Hedges' g at very large degrees of freedom. Earlier releases added an OpenAI-compatible single-model review client and strengthened evidence provenance, semantic-review input validation, Markdown/plain-text section extraction, and negation-aware screening. Directional and causal language checks remain heuristics, not semantic proofs. It also retains the explicit claim-evidence-assumption-method-inference graph and an external semantic-review import/validation workflow. Graph relations are extracted with rules and lexical similarity; they are not proof of semantic support. Imported semantic reviews are structurally validated against source hashes, graph fingerprints, node IDs and source quotes, but the reviewer’s semantic judgment is not independently proven by this software. Existing direction, causality and claim-matching checks remain heuristics. Missing flags do not imply correctness; expert review and independent computational verification remain necessary.

criteria.limitation: Adequacy is a contextual human judgment.

criteria.title: Systematic-review search and retrieval process
required_evidence: Databases, complete queries, dates, coverage, restrictions and search updates.
criteria.procedure: Compare documented searches and protocol with reproducible search records.
criteria.limitation: No comprehensive database search or recall audit is performed.
criteria.applicability_reason: Study type is unknown or mixed; confirm criterion applicability.

criteria.title: Review eligibility, screening and extraction
required_evidence: Eligibility rules, study-flow records, screening decisions and extraction/adjudication forms.
criteria.procedure: Inspect selection/extraction consistency and included-study evidence manually.
criteria.limitation: No automatic study-inclusion or extraction-validity decision is made.
criteria.applicability_reason: Study type is unknown or mixed; confirm criterion applicability.

criteria.title: Applicable evidence pooling and comparability
required_evidence: If pooling is used: study effects/variances, common estimand, dependence assumptions and model.
criteria.procedure: Calculate supported independent pooling, supplied-covariance common-effect GLS, or one group random-intercept REML model.
criteria.limitation: Comparability, sampling covariance/dependence assumptions and study validity are not independently verified.
criteria.applicability_reason: Study type is unknown or mixed; confirm criterion applicability.

criteria.title: Review synthesis and balanced interpretation
required_evidence: Review scope, selection rationale, contradictory findings and justified synthesis.
criteria.procedure: Evaluate synthesis against its sources and stated review approach.
criteria.limitation: No comprehensive semantic synthesis or literature-completeness verification is performed.
criteria.applicability_reason: Study type is unknown or mixed; confirm criterion applicability.

criteria.title: Theoretical proof completeness
required_evidence: Definitions, assumptions, every derivation step, boundary cases and theorem dependencies.
criteria.procedure: Inspect the complete argument and proof obligations with appropriate mathematical expertise.
criteria.limitation: Bounded formula checks cannot certify an entire manuscript proof.
criteria.applicability_reason: Study type is unknown or mixed; confirm criterion applicability.

criteria.title: Definitions and scope of assumptions
required_evidence: Operational/formal definitions, explicit assumptions and their role in each inference.
criteria.procedure: Check that meanings and assumptions are consistent across the manuscript.
criteria.limitation: Implicit assumptions and terminology are not automatically formalized.
criteria.applicability_reason: Included for the declared study type; adequacy still requires human assessment.

criteria.title: Applicable harms and safety reporting
required_evidence: If applicable: harms collection, denominators, timing, severity and reporting scope.
criteria.procedure: Inspect quantified adverse-event cues and compare safety reporting with the protocol.
criteria.limitation: Text cues do not establish safety, complete ascertainment or ethical acceptability.
criteria.applicability_reason: Applicability depends on methods, subjects or claims that require human confirmation.

criteria.title: Applicable full reporting-guideline assessment
required_evidence: Selected study-appropriate guideline, complete item mapping and adequacy judgments.
criteria.procedure: Audit caller-supplied checklist records for quoted evidence, missing mappings and exclusion rationales.
criteria.limitation: Caller-supplied checklist record coverage cannot establish official completeness, relevance or adequacy.
criteria.applicability_reason: Applicability depends on methods, subjects or claims that require human confirmation.

limitations: Original extensible review catalog; not exhaustive or official guideline certification.
Applicability is conditional on caller declarations; not-applicable rows are not independent exclusions.
Evidence pointers show execution or supplied observations, not satisfaction of a scientific criterion.
Source hashes do not establish data authenticity or correct prose-to-formula mapping.
Every scientific verdict remains NOT_ASSESSED, including after successful calculations or model advice.
Unsupported checks and human judgments remain explicit; no scientific completeness or quality score is produced.

reproducibility_manifest.source_code_hash_scope: Python runtime source; JSON schemas; Python tests; Node adapter sources and tests; Build verification tools; Offline pilot recipes and instructions; GitHub Actions workflows; examples; package/build/documentation metadata
reproducibility_manifest.revision_note: The source_code_sha256 covers exactly the relative paths listed in source_code_hash_files; source_code_hash_scope describes their categories. Other repository files are not included.

limitations: Study type is caller-declared, not independently classified.
Other scientific fields can use common checks; specialist coverage is limited to the listed profiles.
Profile cues, arithmetic agreement and model interpretations are not scientific certification.
Only English and Turkish editorial style rules are available; multilingual scientific terminology has uneven coverage.
No independent multi-field expert-labeled accuracy estimate has been established.
